walkthroughs.body_html:
The Global Economy — a core area of Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Global Economy brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Global Economy.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Alfred Marshall published 'Principles of Economics' establishing supply-demand analysis in:
A fall in the price of a substitute good causes demand to:
options: Decrease (curve shifts left)
Increase (shifts right)
Stay constant
Become vertical

mcqs.q: What did Adam Smith mean by the 'invisible hand'?
options: The fiscal multiplier is the rate of growth of the money supply.
The invisible hand refers to government regulating the economy secretly.
That individuals pursuing their own self-interest in competitive markets can unintentionally produce socially beneficial outcomes through the price mechanism.
Adam Smith believed all selfish behaviour always benefits society.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between CPI and RPI as inflation measures?
options: CPI measures consumer prices and RPI measures retail prices — that's the only difference.
The invisible hand refers to government regulating the economy secretly.

Both measure price changes via a basket of goods, but RPI includes housing costs (mortgage interest) and uses an arithmetic mean; CPI excludes housing costs and uses a geometric mean — CPI is the official UK target measure.
CPI and RPI always give the same inflation figure.

mcqs.q: What determines the size of the fiscal multiplier?
options: The invisible hand refers to government regulating the economy secretly.
The fiscal multiplier is always 2 or 3.
The fiscal multiplier is the rate of growth of the money supply.
Mainly the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) — the higher the share of extra income people spend domestically, the bigger the multiplier. Leakages (saving, imports, taxes) reduce the multiplier.
